A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MEG speech-decoding work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial experimental revisions.

before.justification: V1 reports original speech-detection and voicing experiments, including scaling, subject generalisation, supervised benchmarks, and appendix sensitivity analyses.

after.justification: V3 reports original experiments comparing representations, scaling pretraining data, generalising to unseen subjects, and combining pretraining datasets.

M1.justification: V3 standardises downstream training on frozen-backbone linear probing, an option already evaluated in v1 Table 2, and drops the described MLP/deep-fine-tuning variants. It specifies FiLM conditioning. The cortex encoder, three pretext transformations, and combined pretraining objective remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V3 Section 4.5 adds MOUS as an actual pretraining source and evaluates simultaneous Cam-CAN+MOUS pretraining, substantially extending coverage to aggregation across studies. V1 cites and licenses the Schoffelen dataset but reports no corresponding experiment. The two downstream tasks and Armeni/Gwilliams evaluation datasets remain.

E2.justification: V3 Table 1 adds an evaluated BIOT baseline alongside retained raw-input linear and random-backbone comparisons. The earlier MLP and fully supervised encoder comparisons in v1 Tables 2 and 4 disappear. The no-pretraining comparator also disappears from Figure 3's scaling comparison, although it remains in v3 Table 1.

E3.justification: Balanced accuracy changes to ROC AUC, and v3 uses linear probes trained to completion, usually about 300 epochs; v1 describes 10 epochs for scaling in Section 4.3 and 30 in Appendix B. V3 specifies revised held-out sessions and changes unseen subjects from 08–10 to 1–3. The individual-pretext comparison also changes from Armeni pretraining to the default Cam-CAN pretraining.

E4.justification: V3 adds a direct combined-versus-individual pretext comparison and studies how unseen-subject generalisation scales with unlabelled data. It removes v1's semi-supervised cross-task experiment, conditioning ablation, and appendix sensitivity analyses of sensor proportions, encoder dimension, and window length.

E5.justification: V3 Figures 3–4 introduce fitted scaling trends, adding statistical estimation beyond v1's connected observations. Three random seeds, standard errors for main results, and one-sample one-sided t-tests against chance are retained; there is no reported increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: The balanced-accuracy results are extensively replaced by ROC-AUC results under revised settings, so their values do not establish direct performance gains. V3 Table 1 newly reports BIOT at 0.500/0.499 and combined pretext tasks at 0.621/0.543 for Armeni/Gwilliams. Table 2 reports pooled pretraining at 0.611/0.546 versus Cam-CAN alone at 0.621/0.543. Earlier supervised, semi-supervised, and sensitivity result entries are removed.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions of the three pretext losses and their weighted combination in Equations 1–4 remain unchanged. The new scaling-law discussion concerns empirical fits and introduces no formal scaling theorem, derivation, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract replaces its faster-learning claim with claims of superior representations relative to raw inputs and comparable self-supervised approaches. The introduction explicitly adds evidence for scaling laws and emphasises MEG data efficiency. These materially extend the claimed contributions while retaining the central cross-dataset, task, and subject generalisation claim.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations for BIOT's failure involving sensor dimensionality, task difficulty, and data requirements, and attributes mixed dataset-aggregation outcomes to possible data-quality differences. It removes interpretations about labelled-task overspecialisation and conditioning effects from v1. Appendix A newly qualifies held-out-session evaluation by acknowledging possible repetition of training tasks; the main limitations paragraph is largely retained.

D1.justification: V3 adds a statement that supplementary code and reproduction instructions are provided, although those materials are outside the supplied PDFs. It updates hardware to V100/A100 GPUs and revises maximum pretraining time from approximately 150 to 200 hours and final-experiment compute from 2,000 to 3,000 hours. Search-procedure details are removed, but final hyperparameter values and licensing information remain.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds BIOT as a close predecessor and distinguishes its contrastive transformer approach from the proposed method. It also expands discussion of Défossez et al.'s limitations concerning new subjects, datasets, and missing audio labels. The Bordes et al. citation disappears with the encoder-width discussion; most research positioning is retained.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is extensively rewritten and reorganised around linear probing, scaling, and dataset aggregation. Section 3.1 is consolidated and reordered, and the appendices are substantially restructured. Broader Impacts moves into an Ethics Statement, a Reproducibility Statement is added, and acknowledgments and funding text are removed.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to depict the frozen encoder and separate probe. Figure 3 gains ROC-AUC axes, error bars, fitted lines, and prior-study data-volume markers; Figure 4 now displays unseen-subject scaling. Result tables are rebuilt, several appendix tables disappear, and the retained hyperparameter table is relocated and renumbered. Typography and running headers also change throughout.

improvement.justification: V3 strengthens direct assessment of the central representation and scaling claims through standardised linear probing, explicit held-out sessions, BIOT comparison, unseen-subject scaling, and actual pooled-dataset pretraining. These gains are partly offset by removal of useful conditioning, sensitivity, and semi-supervised evidence. Pooling helps only slightly on Gwilliams and hurts Armeni relative to Cam-CAN alone, with reported significance tests addressing chance rather than the pooling advantage. The net quality gain is therefore limited.
